points.t: Facial papules and pustules in a baby. **Comedones** = true acne; pustules without comedones = **cephalic pustulosis**.
Sebaceous glands driven by **maternal and neonatal androgens**, plus *Cutibacterium*.
Neonatal: **observe**, gentle cleansing. Infantile: **BPO ± topical retinoid**. No tetracyclines under 12.
Acne **between ages 1 and 6**, signs of hyperandrogenism, or nodular / scarring disease: refer.

cause.lead: Androgens switch the glands on briefly.
points: Overactive sebaceous glands respond to **maternal and neonatal androgens**.
Same cascade as later acne: plugging, *Cutibacterium*, inflammation.
Androgen drive falls after infancy and rises at adrenarche, so **mid-childhood acne (1–6 years) is very rare** and suggests an endocrine cause.

visuals.caption: The same follicle steps as teenage acne: a plug forms, then inflammation. True acne needs comedones.

points: **Neonatal acne** (birth–6 weeks): ~20% of newborns; papules, pustules ± comedones; usually no scarring.
**Infantile acne** (6 weeks–12–16 months): comedones, papules, pustules, occasional nodules; **may scar**; boys > girls; mainly cheeks.
**Neonatal cephalic pustulosis**: pustules **without true comedones**, often *Malassezia*.

visuals.caption: Neonatal acne: small papules and pustules on the cheeks, chin and forehead of a well baby, with a few tiny comedones. It is not caused by poor hygiene.
visuals.alt: Newborn face with small papules on cheeks

items.name: Cephalic pustulosis / neonatal acne
items.t: Facial papules and pustules in the first weeks.

points: Look for fast growth, early puberty signs, hirsutism, body odour.
Mid-childhood or severe unresponsive acne → endocrinology.

cards.name: Cephalic pustulosis
cards.clue: No or few comedones; may respond to topical antifungal.

cards.name: Periorificial dermatitis
cards.clue: Around mouth and eyes; often steroid-related.

manage.lead: Most clear alone; treat only infantile acne that needs it.

points: **Observe**; gentle cleansing; avoid greasy, comedogenic products.
**Benzoyl peroxide ± topical retinoid** (adapalene or tretinoin) as tolerated; check age licence.
Dermatology: specialists may use isotretinoin in infants.

items.t: **Mid-childhood acne (1–6 years)** or signs of hyperandrogenism (fast growth, body odour, pubic hair, clitoromegaly).
Nodular or scarring disease, or treatment failure.

pearls.t: Reassure: not caused by poor hygiene.
Don’t use adult OTC acne kits on infants without checking age licences.
Persistent facial pustules in a neonate: think cephalic pustulosis.

quiz.q: Neonatal vs infantile acne: age ranges?
quiz.a: Neonatal: birth to ~6 weeks. Infantile: ~6 weeks to 12–16 months.

quiz.q: Which oral antibiotic class to avoid under 12?

quiz.a: Very rare: look for hyperandrogenism and refer to endocrinology.
